title: 2 Kings 7:12–20
context: The king suspects a Syrian ambush, but scouts follow a trail of discarded garments and equipment to the Jordan and confirm the flight (7:12–15). The people plunder the camp, and the prices Elisha announced come true “according to the LORD’s word” (7:16). The captain who scoffed is trampled in the gate and dies, just as the man of God had said (7:17). The narrator then repeats the prophecy and the captain’s reply word for word (7:18–19) before restating the outcome (7:20), underlining that both the promise and the warning were fulfilled exactly. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground about the reliability of the LORD’s word. The captain’s death is presented soberly as the fulfillment of the word he refused to believe, not as a spectacle.

verses.text: The king arose in the night, and said to his servants, “I will now show you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the field, saying, ‘When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive, and get into the city.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The king suspects an ambush, reasoning that the Syrians are hiding in the field. Arminian readers note that his caution, though understandable, reflects the same distrust of God’s word that marked his earlier despair (6:33). He interprets events without reference to Elisha’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the king assumes a human strategy behind the empty camp and does not connect it to the LORD’s word. God’s deliverance can be doubted even when it is at the gate. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing how fear and unbelief can misread God’s gracious acts.

verses.text: One of his servants answered, “Please let some people take five of the horses that remain, which are left in the city. Behold, they are like all the multitude of Israel who are left in it. Behold, they are like all the multitude of Israel who are consumed. Let’s send and see.”
verses.arminianNotes: A servant suggests sending some of the remaining horses to look, since they will die anyway. Arminian readers note the wisdom of a practical, low-risk test. The servant’s proposal moves the king from suspicion to inquiry, and God’s provision is confirmed through ordinary human prudence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see God using a servant’s sensible counsel to bring the king to the truth. The repetition about the multitude of Israel stresses how little the city has left to lose. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of good counsel that serves God’s purpose.

verses.text: Therefore they took two chariots with horses; and the king sent them out to the Syrian army, saying, “Go and see.”
verses.arminianNotes: Two chariots with horses go out at the king’s command: “Go and see.” Arminian readers note the king’s willingness to act on his servant’s advice. The scouting mission allows the truth to be verified, and the king’s response becomes part of how the city is saved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the king’s order simply uncovers what God has already accomplished. Verification follows deliverance rather than producing it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a practical step that confirms the LORD’s rescue, with no theological dispute raised.

verses.text: They went after them to the Jordan; and behold, all the path was full of garments and equipment which the Syrians had cast away in their haste. The messengers returned and told the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The scouts follow a trail of garments and equipment all the way to the Jordan. Arminian readers note the vivid evidence of panic, confirming the lepers’ report. The Syrians’ haste shows how thoroughly God’s action changed the situation in a single night.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scattered equipment as a visible sign of the LORD’s victory over a powerful enemy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confirmation of what God did in 7:6–7, giving the king and the city clear evidence that the siege has ended.

verses.text: The people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, according to the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: The people plunder the camp, and flour and barley sell at the very prices Elisha announced, “according to the LORD’s word.” Arminian readers note that God kept his promise to a city whose king had doubted him. The fulfillment calls for renewed trust in his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the narrator’s explicit statement that everything happened according to the LORD’s word. God’s promises are fulfilled exactly and on time. Shared ground: both traditions read this verse as the center of the passage: the LORD’s word stands, just as he said.

verses.text: The king had appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to be in charge of the gate; and the people trampled over him in the gate, and he died as the man of God had said, who spoke when the king came down to him.
verses.arminianNotes: The captain is placed in charge of the gate and is trampled by the crowd, dying as the man of God had said. Arminian readers see the sober consequence of his refusal to believe. He saw the plenty he had mocked but did not share in it, just as he was warned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fulfillment of God’s word of judgment as precisely as his word of blessing. Shared ground: both traditions read the captain’s death soberly, as the outcome the prophet announced, without delighting in it, and both affirm that God’s warnings are as reliable as his promises.

verses.text: It happened as the man of God had spoken to the king, saying, “Two seahs of barley for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, shall be tomorrow about this time in the gate of Samaria;”
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator repeats Elisha’s promise about barley and flour. Arminian readers note that the repetition invites the reader to compare prophecy and fulfillment line by line. The careful restatement underlines the reliability of the word God spoke through his prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the repetition as deliberate emphasis on fulfillment. Ancient narrative often repeats key words to fix them in memory. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stressing that what God said came about exactly as he said it, so that the reader may trust his word.

verses.text: and that captain answered the man of God, and said, “Now, behold, if the LORD made windows in heaven, might such a thing be?” and he said, “Behold, you will see it with your eyes, but will not eat of it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The captain’s scoffing reply and Elisha’s warning are repeated word for word. Arminian readers note that the narrator keeps the captain’s responsibility in view: he heard the promise, rejected it, and was warned. The repetition highlights unbelief as the reason for his exclusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the repetition of both the unbelief and the warning, presenting the outcome as the fulfillment of God’s word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reminder that God’s word of warning, like his word of promise, deserves to be heard and believed.

verses.text: It happened like that to him, for the people trampled over him in the gate, and he died.
verses.arminianNotes: “It happened like that to him.” Arminian readers note the brief, sober close. The captain’s end confirms the warning without elaboration, and the narrator leaves the lesson for the reader: God’s word should be trusted, not mocked, by those who hear it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the restraint of the narration and the certainty of God’s word. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse as confirming that the LORD’s word was fulfilled in judgment as well as in deliverance, and both handle the captain’s death soberly rather than as a spectacle.
